html:
A huge lion with a human head, carved from the limestone bedrock of the Giza plateau beside the pyramids, on the edge of modern Cairo. It is about 73 metres long and 20 metres high, the largest statue cut from a single mass of rock in the world.

Most Egyptologists date it to the reign of Khafre, around 2500 BCE, in Old Kingdom Egypt. It lies beside his valley temple and causeway, and its face is thought to be his. The builders shaped it from a knob of rock left by quarrying for the pyramids, close to the Great Pyramid of his father Khufu.

Later Egyptians worshipped it as a form of the sun god of the horizon. Sand buried it to the shoulders for much of its history. King Thutmose IV cleared it around 1400 BCE and set up a stele between its paws telling how the Sphinx promised him the throne in a dream. The nose was gone long before Napoleon's army arrived, so the story that his soldiers shot it off is a myth.
